explanation_text: A Dong drum tower rises in stacked tiers, and each tier sits at its own height just as each digit in a number sits in its own place. The higher the tier, the greater the value it holds, and the same is true of digits.
image_prompt: Illustrate a Zhaoxing drum tower with its tiers labeled ones, tens, and hundreds, showing how height changes value.

explanation_text: When a family nets more fish from its paddy field, the catch grows—that is addition. When some fish are given away to relatives, the count falls—that is subtraction.
image_prompt: Show a paddy field where fish are being added to a basket and later given away, with the totals changing.

explanation_text: Transplanting rice in equal rows across a paddy shows multiplication, because the same number is repeated many times. Splitting the harvested bundles evenly among households shows division.
image_prompt: Display even rows of rice seedlings in a paddy, showing equal grouping (multiplication) and even sharing (division).

explanation_text: Fish are often strung two by two on a carrying pole. When every fish has a partner the count is even; a single unmatched fish makes the count odd.
image_prompt: Show paddy fish strung in pairs on a pole, with one single fish at the end to represent an odd number.

explanation_text: Climbing a drum tower by taking every other step—2, 4, 6, 8—is skip counting. The even-spaced railings and floors repeat in a steady rhythm, just like a number pattern.
image_prompt: Show the spiral stair of a drum tower with every fifth step highlighted to illustrate skip counting.

explanation_text: Zhaoxing has five drum towers of different heights. Comparing which is taller and which is shorter is like comparing numbers with greater-than and less-than.
image_prompt: Show the five drum towers of Zhaoxing arranged by height, with > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: Before harvesting, a Dong farmer estimates about how many baskets of rice the paddy will give. Rounding to a convenient number is a quick way to plan ahead.
image_prompt: Show a farmer looking over a golden paddy and estimating baskets, with rounded amounts written on the baskets.

explanation_text: When one steamed fish is shared equally among the family, each person receives a fraction of the whole fish. The fish is the whole, and each equal share names its part.
image_prompt: Show a whole fish on a festival plate divided into equal portions, each labeled as a fraction of the whole.

explanation_text: Cutting a rice cake into 2 equal halves or into 4 equal quarters gives the same total amount. Two halves and four quarters describe the same share, like equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show a sticky rice cake divided first into halves, then quarters, demonstrating equal portions.

explanation_text: A weaver bundles bamboo strips four at a time into larger bunches. Saying 2 bunches of 4 strips or 1 bunch of 8 strips names the same number of strips, like simplifying a fraction.
image_prompt: Depict bundles of bamboo strips merging into larger groups, labeled with reduced fractions.

dong_culture: Full and half baskets of rice
explanation_text: If a home stores 3 full baskets of rice and one half-full basket more, that is 3½ baskets—a whole number joined with a fraction, just like a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three full rice baskets and one half-filled basket labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When the rice harvest fills one basket and overflows into a second measured in the same units, the total is more than one whole basket—an improper fraction.
image_prompt: Show several rice baskets filled beyond one full portion, symbolizing fractions greater than 1.

explanation_text: Pouring portions of pickled fish from two small jars into one larger jar shows how fractional amounts add together to make a whole.
image_prompt: Show smaller jars of pickled fish being combined into one total jar.

dong_culture: Serving part of a soup pot
explanation_text: Ladling out part of a big pot of Dong sour-soup leaves a fractional part behind. Removing a portion is subtracting a fraction from the whole.
image_prompt: Show a pot of sour soup with a portion being ladled out, the remainder labeled as the fraction left.

explanation_text: If each guest is offered half of half a portion of glutinous rice, you are finding a fraction of a fraction—like multiplying fractions.
image_prompt: Show a bowl of glutinous rice divided into halves, and one half divided again to show smaller portions.

explanation_text: When a flat corn cake is cut into small even pieces, you ask how many small pieces fit into the whole—that is dividing a fraction by another fraction.
image_prompt: Show a corn cake being cut into smaller even pieces to illustrate fractional division.

dong_culture: Measuring rice in jin and liang
explanation_text: Rice is weighed in jin (斤) and liang (两), where ten liang make one jin. A weight like 1.5 jin means one jin plus half a jin, just like reading a decimal.
image_prompt: Show a beam scale weighing rice at 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 jin.

explanation_text: Whether you say half a basket of rice or 0.5 basket, both describe the same amount. Speaking the same quantity in two ways is like converting fractions and decimals.
image_prompt: Show two rice baskets, one marked ½ and another marked 0.5, holding the same amount.

explanation_text: When a student scores 90 out of 100 on a Mandarin exam at a Qiandongnan school, that is 90%—a way to express parts per hundred.
image_prompt: Show a test paper with 90/100 written and a 90% mark beside it.

explanation_text: A 10% discount on indigo cloth at the Sanjiang market shows how percents are used to find a part of a number.
image_prompt: Show a market stall sign with indigo cloth marked '10% off' and price tags with reduced amounts.

explanation_text: A net pulled from the paddy may hold a fish you have not counted yet. An unknown amount stands in for it, just like a variable in math.
image_prompt: Show a fish basket with a labeled count (5) and an unlabeled basket marked as x.

explanation_text: If you have 2 full baskets of rice and x more waiting to be filled, that is like writing the expression 2 + x.
image_prompt: Show two rice baskets plus one unfilled basket, symbolized as 2 + x.

explanation_text: When the two ends of a carrying scale hold equal weight, the pole hangs level. Equality between two sides is exactly what an equation states.
image_prompt: Show a beam scale with equal baskets on both sides labeled as an equation.

explanation_text: If one end of a carrying pole sags, you add or remove one basket to level it again. One careful adjustment is like solving a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a carrying pole with balanced baskets on both ends illustrating equal sides.

explanation_text: Making zongzi for Dong New Year needs two actions in order: wrapping the rice first, then steaming it. Solving a two-step equation also means doing two steps in the right order.
image_prompt: Show the step sequence: wrap the zongzi, then steam it, then enjoy the result, symbolizing step-by-step solving.

explanation_text: When one family's rice harvest is larger than a neighbor's, the two amounts are not equal. That difference is shown with a greater-than or less-than sign.
image_prompt: Show two stacks of rice baskets of different sizes with > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: To make sweet fermented rice you must steam the glutinous rice before adding the fermenting starter. The order of steps matters, just as operations have a fixed order in math.
image_prompt: Show a sequence where rice must be steamed before fermenting, labeled like parentheses, exponents, and so on.

explanation_text: When one worn beam of a wind and rain bridge is replaced with an identical new one, the bridge holds as before. Swapping in a matching part is like substituting a value for a variable.
image_prompt: Show a wind and rain bridge beam being replaced by an identical one, representing substitution.

explanation_text: Each lantern hanging along a wind and rain bridge marks one position, like a point marking a location in geometry.
image_prompt: Show a bridge lined with lanterns, with individual lanterns labeled as points on a coordinate grid.

explanation_text: The long wooden beams that run the length of a wind and rain bridge stretch straight ahead, just like geometric lines that extend in both directions.
image_prompt: Show the long straight beams of a wind and rain bridge, representing geometric lines.

explanation_text: When a lattice window on a drum tower swings open, the door and its frame form an angle between them.
image_prompt: Show a drum tower lattice window open at an angle, with the angle clearly marked.

explanation_text: The wooden pillars of a wind and rain bridge rise straight up to meet the deck, forming perpendicular lines and strong right angles that hold the roof.
image_prompt: Show wind and rain bridge pillars meeting the deck at 90-degree angles.

explanation_text: The twin rows of beams along a wind and rain bridge run side by side at a constant distance and never meet, like parallel lines.
image_prompt: Show two rows of beams running side by side along a covered bridge.

explanation_text: Seen from below, the layered roofs of a drum tower form closed many-sided shapes, from octagons to hexagons to squares.
image_prompt: Show the overhead shapes of several drum tower roofs forming geometric patterns.

dong_culture: Tier brackets of the drum tower
explanation_text: Each tier of a drum tower is held up by triangular wooden brackets. Every bracket has three sides and gives the tower its strength.
image_prompt: Show the triangular bracket segments that support each tier of a drum tower.

dong_culture: Lattice windows of the drum tower
explanation_text: The carved lattice windows and wooden panels on a drum tower are full of four-sided shapes—squares, rectangles, and trapezoids.
image_prompt: Show a drum tower with repeating square and rectangular lattice motifs.

explanation_text: Walking all the way around the base gallery of a drum tower measures its distance around—exactly what the perimeter of a shape tells you.
image_prompt: Show people walking around the base of a drum tower with a dashed line tracing the perimeter.

explanation_text: The amount of land a paddy field covers is its area, often measured in mu (亩). A larger field holds more rice, just as a larger area holds more space.
image_prompt: Show terraced Dong paddy fields in a valley, one field shaded to show its area.

explanation_text: The amount of rice a round wooden grain bin can hold is its volume. Deeper and wider bins hold more grain, just as volume measures the space inside a shape.
image_prompt: Show round wooden grain bins filled to different levels to illustrate volume.

dong_culture: Looking down into the drum tower
explanation_text: Looking down from the top of a drum tower shows its round interior as a circle, revealing the radius, diameter, and circumference all at once.
image_prompt: Show a drum tower interior from above labeled with radius and diameter lines.

explanation_text: The round gallery rail of a drum tower is about 3.14 times as long across as it is wide through the center. That fixed ratio is pi (π).
image_prompt: Show a circular drum tower floor labeled with circumference and diameter measurements.

explanation_text: The beams of a wind and rain bridge cross in a regular grid, like a coordinate plane. Each crossing point can be named by its row and column.
image_prompt: Show a wind and rain bridge timber grid labeled with x and y coordinates.

dong_culture: Mapping paddy plots of the village
explanation_text: Marking where each family's paddy plot lies on a village map is like plotting points on a coordinate plane.
image_prompt: Show a village map with labeled paddy plots marked as points on a grid.

explanation_text: A wind and rain bridge and its reflection in the river are mirror images across the waterline, a perfect example of symmetry.
image_prompt: Show a wind and rain bridge reflected in the river, with a mirror line at the water's surface.

dong_culture: Dancers circling at the lusheng festival
explanation_text: When dancers circle and turn during a lusheng festival performance, the whole formation shifts, rotates, and mirrors—like geometric transformations.
image_prompt: Show lusheng dancers turning and shifting positions to illustrate transformations.

dong_culture: Mixing indigo dye for ziyin cloth
explanation_text: Dyeing ziyin cloth mixes indigo and water in a fixed balance, such as two parts dye to one part water. That balance is a ratio.
image_prompt: Show an indigo dyeing vat labeled with a dye-to-water ratio, like 2:1.

explanation_text: When a weaver copies a small rice-flower embroidery onto a larger cloth while keeping every part in the same ratio, that is maintaining proportion.
image_prompt: Show a small and a large rice-flower embroidery with the same geometric proportions.

explanation_text: The number of rice seedlings a farmer plants in one day is a unit rate, such as 300 seedlings per day.
image_prompt: Show a farmer planting rice seedlings with a rate written as seedlings per day.

explanation_text: A master carpenter draws a smaller plan of a drum tower while keeping every measurement in proportion, a classic scale drawing.
image_prompt: Show a drum tower and a smaller scaled plan side by side with a scale legend.

explanation_text: If a village's paddy fish harvest rises from 100 to 120 baskets, that is a 20% increase—a clear example of percent change.
image_prompt: Show a harvest growing in baskets with a +20% label.

explanation_text: Recording how many fish each paddy field produces is a simple act of data collection, the first step of every survey.
image_prompt: Show a villager marking tallies of fish on a wooden counting board.

explanation_text: Using a graph to show how much rice each village harvests makes the comparison easy to see at a glance.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph comparing rice harvests across nearby Dong villages.

explanation_text: Finding the average amount of rice each paddy field produces gives the mean, a single number that summarizes many fields.
image_prompt: Show a table of paddy yields with the average value highlighted.

dong_culture: Middle fish catch of the week
explanation_text: When a week's fish catches are listed from smallest to largest, the catch in the middle is the median.
image_prompt: Show daily fish catches lined up with the middle one highlighted as the median.

dong_culture: Most common fish in the paddy
explanation_text: If most of the fish in a paddy are carp, then carp is the mode of the catch—the value that appears most often.
image_prompt: Show fish of several kinds with carp being the most common.

explanation_text: The gap between the largest and smallest harvest in a village is the range, a single number that shows how spread out the data is.
image_prompt: Show a bar chart with the shortest and tallest bars marked to show the range.

explanation_text: Each bar in the chart shows how many fish one family caught, making it quick to compare all families side by side.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph labeled by family names with their fish harvest totals.

dong_culture: Tracking paddy water through the year
explanation_text: A line graph shows how the water level in a paddy field rises and falls with the seasons across the year.
image_prompt: Show a line graph labeled with months and paddy water levels.

explanation_text: A pie chart can show the proportion of rice, vegetables, and fish ponds around a Dong village, with each slice a percent of the whole.
image_prompt: Show a pie chart divided into crop categories with percentages.

explanation_text: Before a Grand Song festival, guessing which village choir is most likely to win involves probability—estimating how likely each outcome is.
image_prompt: Show Grand Song choirs at a festival with probability labels above each.

explanation_text: In the Grand Song, voices enter one after another in repeating rounds, each part joining at its turn—a musical pattern of repetition and order.
image_prompt: Show Grand Song singers with entering voice parts repeating in a round.

explanation_text: In a Grand Song round, each singer takes one part and produces one melody. Every input gives exactly one output—that is what a function means.
image_prompt: Show a diagram linking each singer (input) to one melody part (output).
